title: The Last Electron Rule Explained Simply | PUC Chemistry Class 11
description:
A city is split into blocks, a school into sections, a market into aisles. Split a big crowd by kind and it becomes easy to find your way. The periodic table does the same with four blocks. In this animated lesson for PUC and Class 11 Chemistry (NCERT Chapter 3, Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties) we learn to tell an element's block from one clue: where its last electron goes.

You will see periods (rows that fill one outer shell) and groups (columns with the same outer arrangement) light up on a hand-built periodic table, then the s, p, d and f blocks colour in, 2, 6, 10 and 14 columns wide because s, p, d and f subshells hold 2, 6, 10 and 14 electrons. On the molecule bench the last electron of sodium, chlorine, iron and europium drops into its orbital, with the outer configuration of each block (ns1-2, ns2 np1-6, (n-1)d1-10 ns0-2, (n-2)f1-14 (n-1)d0-1 ns2). We look at helium, the odd case, then place four elements by configuration, the iron exam trap, an original NEET pattern question with a full solution, a recap card and three questions to check yourself.

This is Episode 29 of our PUC Chemistry series.

Made for PUC (Karnataka), CBSE Class 11, NEET and JEE Main students.

In this video:

0:34 Periods and groups: the map
0:54 The four blocks: s, p, d, f
1:02 Why the blocks are 2, 6, 10 and 14 wide
1:15 The last electron on the molecule bench
2:24 Helium, the odd case + pause and think
2:53 Worked example: place four elements
3:39 Exam trap: iron is not s-block
4:04 Practice question (NEET pattern)
4:38 Recap and three questions to answer

Next episode: Electronic Configuration and Position of Elements. Can you find an element's address from its electrons alone?
